video_title: Banks Could Lose 30% of Their Profits with Christian Schmid (Managing Director, BCG)
gist: Christian Schmid, BCG's global banking lead and lead author of its flagship digital-asset report, explains BCG's model showing up to 15% of bank revenues and 30% of bank profits at risk by 2035 from stablecoins and tokenization, but argues the asset-management opportunity is actually bigger than the threat, that the real battleground is the consumer interface (illustrated by Aave's yield-bearing stablecoin app) rather than deposits per se, and that most banks still lack a real strategy despite near-universal awareness.

themes.theme: The 30% Profit Threat — Mechanism and Scope

insights.claim: BCG's model estimates that in a scenario of strong non-bank-driven digital asset adoption (heavy stablecoin use, tokenized real-world assets, regulation catching up), banks face up to 15% of revenues and 30% of profits at risk by 2035 versus a status-quo baseline.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Gives investors a quantified downside case for bank equities under a fast digital-asset-adoption scenario; Schmid himself flags it as a simulation, not a forecast, so treat it as a scenario anchor rather than a point estimate.
insights.quote: so you come to these numbers of 30% of profits at risk in 10 years from now and also 15% of revenues

insights.claim: The profit hit is a 'double whammy': transaction-banking fee income and net-interest-margin on deposits erode as activity and deposits migrate to stablecoins, while banks simultaneously incur new costs to build and maintain 'dual rails' (both legacy and digital-asset infrastructure).
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Bank margin compression from digital assets is not just a revenue story — infrastructure duplication cost is a distinct, compounding headwind worth modeling separately in bank cost projections.
insights.quote: it's almost a bit the double whammy

insights.claim: Schmid says the 15%/30% figures are industry-wide averages and that every bank must run this threat/opportunity analysis for its own specific business mix and regions, since the impact will vary sharply bank to bank.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Investors comparing bank stocks on digital-asset exposure should weight by each bank's transaction-banking and deposit-funding mix rather than applying a flat industry discount.
insights.quote: every bank has a specific business profile in specific regions and so this type of number is for the whole industry but it might look quite different from bank to bank

insights.claim: Schmid pushes back on the crypto-native 'banks are being replaced' narrative: clients are not demanding stablecoins or tokenized deposits from their banks, and most people don't want to self-custody funds in a wallet like MetaMask — they want a trusted institution holding the keys, which remains a structural moat for banks.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Trust/custody remains a defensible bank franchise value even in an aggressive digital-asset adoption scenario — an offset investors should weigh against the headline profit-at-risk number.
insights.quote: I don't put all my money in my MetaMask wallet with a you know self-managed key but I rather put it in a trusty bank which kind of manages the key for me

themes.theme: Opportunity Outweighs Threat — Asset Management & Trading

insights.claim: BCG's model finds the asset-management opportunity from tokenization is larger than the profit threat: wrapping more of the world's assets into fee-earning tokenized structures, plus easier global distribution via DLT's inherent reach, is projected to grow total assets under management and asset managers' fee pools.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Asset managers, not just banks, should be viewed as net beneficiaries of tokenization in BCG's model — a differentiated read versus the doom narrative applied to financial incumbents generally.

insights.claim: On trading, BCG expects a mixed effect similar to the ETF era — higher trading volumes but compressed fees that roughly net out — with the more consequential change being that tokenized trading needs far less capital and liquidity, which lifts return on equity for large trading organizations.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Capital efficiency, not fee revenue, is the more durable trading-business upside from tokenization — relevant for handicapping bank ROE trajectories at large sell-side trading franchises.

insights.claim: Schmid frames technology adoption with a standard pattern he's seen repeatedly in 27 years of banking consulting: the effect is overestimated in the short term and underestimated in the long term. BCG's own model shows little financial impact from digital assets in the next 5 years, with the real divergence in profitability opening up between adopting and non-adopting banks only after that.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Sets an actionable time horizon: don't expect near-term (0-5yr) P&L impact from digital assets at banks, but expect a widening performance spread among banks starting roughly mid-decade-plus.
insights.quote: you overestimate the effect in the short term and you underestimate it in the long term

insights.claim: Schmid cites Revolut as the precedent for underestimating long-term disruption: incumbent bank executives mocked its years of losses during the neobank/mobile-banking wave, yet roughly a decade later its market capitalization (or potential market cap) exceeds many of the biggest established banks.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: A concrete precedent for why incumbents dismissing early-stage digital-asset challengers on current unprofitability could repeat the same mistake they made with neobanks.
insights.quote: now like 10 years later they have a market capitalization or a potential market capitalization which is bigger than many of the biggest banks

insights.claim: Schmid argues digital-asset technology could be even more fundamental than the prior neobank/mobile-banking disruption because it doesn't just change the customer interface — it can change how the monetary system itself works.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Raises the ceiling on how structurally banks could be reshaped versus prior digitization waves — a reason to treat this cycle as qualitatively different, not just another fintech wave.

themes.theme: Three Categories of Digital Assets & Where Value Accrues

insights.claim: Schmid's framework splits digital assets into three distinct categories: (1) tokenized securities/real-world assets, which he expects to be functionally indistinguishable from traditional securities within 20 years; (2) digital money/stablecoins, backed by high-quality assets and comparable to travelers' checks or the post-financial-crisis narrow-banking debate, but never before achieved at scale; and (3) cryptocurrencies proper, which are speculative, not asset-backed, and which BCG does not project significant further growth for (around 2%).
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: A clean investor taxonomy: don't lump tokenized RWAs, stablecoins, and speculative crypto together — BCG's own model treats crypto-proper as the weakest growth category of the three going forward.

insights.claim: Value is migrating away from pure intermediation (layer-1 blockchains, now commoditized and interchangeable) toward issuers and consumers at the application layer — examples cited include a stablecoin cross-border transfer company acquired by Mastercard and infrastructure companies pursuing IPOs, while base-layer tokens are expected to capture much less of the ecosystem's value than they did over the last decade.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid / host, discussing BCG report
insights.so_what: Reframes where to look for digital-asset value capture: application-layer issuers and infrastructure providers, not base-layer token exposure.
insights.quote: value migrates away from pure intermediation towards issuers and consumers

insights.claim: Schmid predicts the real competitive battleground for banks will not be which rail wins (fiat vs. stablecoins vs. tokenized deposits) — consumers don't care about that distinction — but who controls the consumer interface layered on top of these technologies.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Bank digital-asset strategy should prioritize owning distribution/UX, not just backend rail choice — a concrete strategic filter for evaluating bank digital-asset initiatives.

insights.claim: Schmid cites Aave's consumer app (launched a few months before this recording) as the template for the threat: users deposit fiat, it's converted to stablecoins, and a DeFi protocol generates a 5-9% annual yield behind a simple one-click interface — Aave owns both the front-end and back-end, which is why successful crypto-native firms like this then apply for banking licenses to extend into full banking services, and why banks' most urgent first step is enabling clients to hold crypto/digital assets directly with them.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: A concrete competitive benchmark: banks are being out-executed on consumer yield products by DeFi-backed apps with bank-grade simplicity, and are already at risk of losing custody of clients' existing crypto holdings.
insights.quote: generate a 5 to 9% annual yield by using a protocol in the back end but she doesn't need to know that she just clicks a button and gets that yield

insights.claim: Schmid identifies the two currently 'real' (proven, revenue-generating) use cases as: retail/private-banking crypto trading using stablecoins, and institutional collateral mobility/repo financing/atomic settlement of the type JPMorgan's Kinexys platform targets.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Narrows the current addressable, monetizable use-case set for banks to two proven categories, useful for prioritizing near-term digital-asset investment.

insights.claim: Schmid flags store-of-value use in emerging markets and cross-border money transfer to emerging markets as a significant but under-discussed real use case outside Western markets.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: A less crowded, likely underpriced use-case corridor (EM store-of-value/remittances) relative to the Western-market-centric digital-asset narrative.

insights.claim: Trade finance remains, in Schmid's view, a 'use case in search of a problem' — theoretically far more efficient on-chain, but still far off in practice, following unsuccessful earlier pilots.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: A caution flag against over-allocating attention/capital to trade-finance tokenization pitches despite their theoretical appeal.
insights.quote: trade finance you can beautifully imagine how this could be much more efficient but it's just that's a bit more down the road

insights.claim: By now every bank CEO has digital assets on their radar, but execution varies widely: Standard Chartered and JPMorgan (via Kinexys, in a more closed-loop model) are pursuing this publicly and aggressively, while other banks acknowledge its importance but haven't committed to investing the hundreds of millions of dollars needed for digital custody, wallets, and new products.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: A concrete way to screen banks on digital-asset commitment versus rhetoric — a differentiator for relative-value bank stock analysis.

insights.claim: Digital assets compete for bank capital and management attention against AI and the broader shift to private credit/non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs); Schmid ranks reaccelerating CIB (corporate & investment banking) growth first, AI second, and digital assets third among the biggest industry themes he sees.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Digital assets should be modeled as one of at least three simultaneous, capital-competing strategic priorities at banks, not the sole or dominant theme — helps calibrate how much bank capex realistically flows to digital-asset build-out.

insights.claim: Despite the urgency of the topic, Schmid's explicit recommendation to banks is not alarm-driven crash strategy but focused prioritization and disciplined execution; he says a deliberate, consciously-chosen 'wait and see' stance can itself be a legitimate strategy, as long as it isn't just default inertia.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: A contrarian-to-typical-consultant framing: not every bank needs an all-out digital-asset sprint — inaction can be defensible if it's a deliberate, reasoned choice rather than avoidance.
insights.quote: waiting and seeing is not a strategy or it might be a deliberate strategy

insights.claim: BCG's report models four end-state scenarios for digital assets: a no-digital-assets base case (e.g., triggered by a major crypto crisis and regulatory clampdown); a 'private-led' scenario driven by fintechs/crypto-natives with supportive US regulation, which is unfavorable for banks — especially regional banks that can't keep pace; an 'institution-led' scenario where tokenized deposits and CBDCs (in the spirit of Project Agorá) dominate as a modernization of the current system, driven by banks; and a 'fragmented' scenario where different regions diverge due to geopolitics, creating arbitrage opportunities but making it harder to build liquidity, which Schmid says most resembles today's world.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Gives investors a scenario tree to map regulatory/geopolitical developments onto bank-sector winners and losers, rather than treating digital-asset adoption as a single linear path.

insights.claim: BCG's report caps stablecoin growth at an upper boundary of 15% of money supply, roughly $12 trillion by 2035, benchmarked against cash penetration in developed economies and retail money-market fund sizes; Schmid argues full displacement of bank deposits via a narrow-banking-style stablecoin system is implausible absent a wholesale regulatory overhaul of the monetary system.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Puts a hard, sourced ceiling on the stablecoin bull case ($12T by 2035) that investors can use to check more aggressive market-size projections circulating elsewhere.
insights.quote: we basically give an upper boundary of 15% of money supply too which would be if I'm not mistaken around 12 trillion by uh 2035

insights.claim: In the tokenized-deposits-vs-stablecoins race, Schmid says tokenized deposits preserve the current monetary system but require a slow, multi-bank interoperability agenda (e.g., Project Agorá, a recent domestic-payments pilot), while fast-moving fintechs can build and entrench stablecoin-based solutions before banks finish coordinating — meaning stablecoins likely win in hard-to-reach cross-border markets and use cases like derivative margining where no yield is needed.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Speed of coordination, not technical superiority, is the deciding factor in the tokenized-deposit-vs-stablecoin race in specific niches — an argument for why bank consortia (interoperability efforts) are racing the clock against fintech stablecoin issuers.
insights.quote: the fintexs at the moment are just fast and they can build solutions which are then also a bit harder to replace by banks

insights.claim: In the episode's rapid-fire round, Schmid explicitly calls both central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) and 'stablecoins as a threat to banks' overrated.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: A blunt, high-conviction dual contrarian call from a bank-industry insider against two of the most hyped digital-asset narratives — worth weighing against more alarmist stablecoin-vs-bank commentary elsewhere.

insights.claim: Asked what is most slowing institutional tokenization — technology, regulation, demand, or trust — Schmid answered that all four factors are simultaneously constraining it, not just one.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Warns against single-cause explanations (e.g., 'it's just regulation') for slow institutional tokenization adoption — all four levers need to move together.

insights.claim: Asked whether public or private chains will win for institutional money, Schmid predicted both will coexist rather than one displacing the other.
insights.speaker: Christian Schmid, BCG
insights.so_what: Investors and infrastructure builders shouldn't bet on a winner-take-all outcome between public and private institutional chains.
